name: Palate expander

lead: A palate expander is a fixed appliance, usually cemented to the upper molars, with a central screw that is turned to push the halves of the upper jaw apart. It corrects a narrow upper jaw, crossbite and crowding, most commonly between ages 8 and 18, and gives a wider, roomier smile arch.

Looksmaxxing forums discuss it for a wider midface and better breathing, often asking whether it still works at 16 or 17. Studies report dental arch and skeletal changes; none in the sources reviewed tested effects on general facial attractiveness.

paras: The orthodontist turns the screw (or the family does at home) gradually, and bone fills the gap during several months of retention, often followed by braces. After puberty the suture is more rigid, so adults are often treated with MARPE or surgically assisted expansion.

Reported effects include lisp, extra saliva, pain, headaches, tongue sores, a gap between the upper front teeth and periodontal changes. Some expansion can be lost afterward. It is prescribed and monitored by an orthodontist.

angle.text: Palate expanders widen a narrow upper jaw, mainly in children and teens, and looksmaxxing posters hope for a wider midface and fuller face as well. Widening for crossbite and narrow palates is well established; facial-appearance effects are largely unstudied.

lead: A palate expander (also called a rapid palatal expander, RPE or RME) is an orthodontic appliance that widens the upper jaw. A screw mechanism, usually anchored to the upper molars, is activated gradually to separate the midpalatal suture and increase maxillary width [1].

It is mainly used to correct a narrow upper jaw with posterior crossbite, crowding and some airway concerns, and is most common in ages 8 to 18; it is generally believed to work best before or around the pubertal growth spurt [1]. Expanders are also used in cleft lip and palate patients [2][3] and in combination with facemask treatment for Class III malocclusion [4].

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to widen the midface and palate and to improve breathing [5][6]. Published studies report dental arch and skeletal changes; no study in the sources reviewed has tested effects on general facial attractiveness.
infobox: Fixed orthodontic appliance (Hyrax, Haas, quad-helix, others)
About 3 to 6 months after active expansion [1]

paras: Conventional rapid expanders are tooth-borne: bands on the upper molars connect to a central jackscrew that the patient or parent turns, typically over a few weeks, until a crossbite is corrected, after which the appliance stays in place while bone fills the gap [1]. Slow expansion devices exist that apply lighter, longer-lasting force, and Wikipedia reports they produce a more even mix of dental and skeletal change with less discomfort [1].

Named designs include the Hyrax (introduced by Biederman in 1968), the Haas expander, the quad-helix and nickel-titanium expanders [1][7]. Hybrid designs combine dental anchorage with miniscrews, including a modified expander described in a young patient with ectodermal dysplasia [8]. Mini-implant-supported variants such as MARPE are used where the suture is less easily opened [1].

Wikipedia credits Emerson C. Angell with the first paper on palatal expansion in 1860, with later milestones including Haas reintroducing his expander in the United States in 1956 and the Hyrax in 1968 [1]. Patents for palate expanders, including a 2001 US patent, are also on record [9].

A retrospective clinical trial of 28 cleft lip and palate patients in mixed dentition compared a rapid palatal expander with a quad-helix [2]. A 2025 study used stereophotogrammetry and intraoral scans to examine soft tissue and dental arch effects of rapid palate expansion in cleft patients [3]. A preliminary study of children with skeletal Class III compared using a protraction facemask before or after rapid palatal expansion [4].

Finite element studies have modelled stress distribution in the maxillary complex with different expanders [7][10]. Case reports describe hybrid expanders with miniscrews [8]. Wikipedia notes that older studies reported a portion of the expansion being lost before the result stabilised [1].
No trial in the sources reviewed has measured whether expansion in otherwise healthy teens changes perceived facial attractiveness.

Wikipedia lists speech difficulty (lisp, extra saliva), pain and headaches, tongue sores, a gap between the upper front teeth (diastema) and bone and periodontal changes such as buccal bone fenestration and extrusion of posterior teeth [1]. It also notes that the zygomatic buttress limits posterior expansion, so widening tends to occur more at the front than the back [1].

Teenagers on looksmax.org ask whether palate expanders widen the face or midface, how much expansion is ideal and whether they still work at 16 to 18 [5][6][11]. Some posters ask whether to mention breathing difficulties to qualify for treatment [6], and another thread discusses pairing an expander with reverse-pull headgear [5]. Others say a wide-faced person may look 'uncanny' after expansion [11]. These are individual opinions and anecdotes.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org palate expanders are treated as a gear-based way to widen the maxilla, usually discussed by teenagers and young adults [5][6].
